studies.title: What The Wealth Could Not Do
studies.meaning: The chapter opens with a verb of ruin applied to two hands, then repeated of the man himself, so the instrument and the person are condemned in a single line. The second line states an outcome rather than a sentence: his wealth did not help him, nor what he earned. Commentators read that last phrase as his gains generally or as his children specifically, since Arabic can call offspring what a man has earned, and both readings stand. The final lines turn to his wife, named by an occupation, and to a cord of palm fibre at her neck.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The classical sources report that the man named was a close relative of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and one of the city's leading opponents, and that the chapter answered a public dismissal of the message before a gathering. Kinship was the entire basis of protection in Mecca, so hostility from inside the family was more dangerous than hostility from outside it, and the sources treat that as the setting.

keyTerms.note: A verb of loss and ruin, applied first to hands rather than to a person. Arabic names the part that acted, so what is condemned at the opening is the work those hands had been doing.
The ordinary verb for earning. Commentators read the phrase as covering his gains in general or his children in particular, since Arabic can speak of offspring as something a man has earned.
A cord twisted from the fibre stripped off a palm trunk, the cheapest rope available. The word occurs only here in the Quran, and readings run from that material to a chain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Palm fibre was the poorest cord there was, pulled off the trunk and twisted by hand in an afternoon. It was what you used to tie a bundle of firewood, and gathering firewood was work done by households with nothing else to sell. For a woman of standing in Mecca to be pictured carrying a bundle on a fibre rope was a reversal the first audience would have felt immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the rope's material, the word used for her neck, and the word for the firewood all occur only here in the entire Quran. A chapter of five very short lines therefore contains several words the rest of the Book never uses again, which is one reason the classical lexicographers treat its vocabulary as a set of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Classical commentators note that no other living opponent is named in the Quran in this way, and that the outcome is stated in advance and never withdrawn, which they treat as a claim deliberately staked where it could have been falsified. Beneath that sits a plainer point the chapter makes twice: wealth and earnings are shown simply failing to reach the place they were needed, and closeness to a prophet is shown to confer nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: States the same failure as a general rule, that a man's wealth will not avail him when he falls.
Records the instruction to warn the nearest relatives, which the sources connect to this chapter's occasion.
Gives two earlier cases where closeness to a prophet availed nothing against God at all.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship where being related is doing all the work: where you assume goodwill, or assume you are owed something, because of the name you share. Ask what would be left of it without that. The answer is usually not nothing. But this chapter is about a man for whom it was.
